newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Hun Sen's forces control Cambodian capital.
newsitem.headline: Hun Sen's forces control Cambodian capital.

text.p: Cambodia's Second Prime Minister Hun Sen took complete control of Phnom Penh and its outskirts on Monday, hours after he unilaterally ousted his rival as first prime minister.
Troops loyal to First Premier Prince Norodom Ranariddh pulled out of their Tang Krasang base near Phnom Penh airport overnight, leaving Hun Sen's forces unopposed.

The casualty count was difficult to determine but one government official said it was as high as 150. He could not say how many were dead or wounded but hospital sources said at least 12 people had been killed in two days of fighting in Phnom Penh.

The rest of the country appeared to be quiet on Monday although an official loyal to Ranariddh in the northwestern city of Battambang said there had been a brief clash between the two sides there early on Monday.

Hun Sen said in a radio broadcast late on Sunday that Ranariddh, his uneasy coalition government partner since 1993 elections, was a "traitor and a thief" and said the prince no longer held the post of first prime minister.
Ranariddh left Cambodia on Friday, the eve of the fighting, and was in France, an aide said. A family member also said the prince was in France.
Ranariddh issued a statement there on Saturday denouncing Hun Sen's move against his forces as a coup.
In his radio broadcast, Hun Sen also ruled out any intervention by King Norodom Sihanouk, Ranariddh's father, who is currently in Beijing undergoing medical treatment.
As fighting raged in Phnom Penh over the weekend, the king called for both prime ministers to visit him in Beijing to try to resolve their differences. But Hun Sen said that would not be necessary.
"It is heard that the King proposes to have reconciliation in Beijing," Hun Sen said. "It is too late and it is not necessary. Everything is over."

The fighting erupted in Phnom Penh on Saturday after Hun Sen sent his forces against Ranariddh's men. Hun Sen said the action was necessary because Ranariddh's commandos had been smuggling defectors from the Khmer Rouge guerrilla group into the capital to boost their troop strength.
Fighting was light on Monday. Bursts of small arms fire were heard intermittently around the capital.
Phnom Penh residents could travel freely through the city centre on Monday but many shop and government offices kept their shutters locked. Shoppers reported exorbitant prices.

State television, which has always been under the control of Hun Sen's Cambodian People's Party (CPP), showed pictures of abandoned, bombed-out facilities where men from Ranariddh's royalist FUNCINPEC party had holed up over the weekend.
The French Embassy was among the buildings damaged in the fighting on Sunday. A shell destroyed the ambassador's office and that of the military attache, an embassy official said.

No flights in or out of Phnom Penh were expected on Monday, an airport security official said. One aviation source in Phnom Penh said the airport runway had been damaged by shellfire and it was doubtful commercial airlines could land.
Keo Sophal, the director general of the Civil Aviation Authority, said he hoped the airport would be open by Wednesday.

"Last night illegal forces controlled the airport and broke equipment and looted because they were drunk," he said, referring to forces loyal to Ranariddh. "Now government troops control it again and we will start repairs. We hope to open tomorrow or the day after."
On Monday morning, the airport, shops, houses and warehouses in the area were looted by soldiers, witnesses said.
"Yesterday soldiers, today robbers," said one resident in the area. "FUNCINPEC soldiers took all the duty free and now CPP soldiers are taking what's left," said an airport worker.
Soldiers and civilians also looted warehouses on the airport road and were seen driving off in new cars and on motorbikes. Others were carting off televisions and various appliances.
Military police and soldiers later tried to restore order, firing shots in the air to disperse crowds, witnesses said.
Indonesian Foreign Minister Ali Alatas said he was consulting colleagues in the region to discuss the possibility of an Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) meeting on Cambodia.
Cambodia, Laos and Burma are due to become full members of the association at the end of this month but Philippine Foreign Secretary Domingo Siazon told reporters ASEAN could still change its mind.
"That decision could still change depending on how bad the situation turns out," he said.
Malaysia's Acting Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said the ASEAN position on Cambodia had not changed "because the commitment has already been made".
ASEAN comprises Malaysia, the Philippines, Indonesia, Singapore, Thailand, Brunei and Vietnam.
